# **Abstract**

Background  
Nonsense-mediated decay (NMD) destroys aberrant messenger RNA (mRNA) transcripts following ribosomal engagement. In eukaryotic cells, NMD degrades \~15% of all mRNA, and NMD, in concert with alternative splicing, plays a fundamental role in the regulation of protein expression levels. While premature termination codons (PTCs) are well-established triggers of NMD, the transcript-wide sequence and splicing determinants of NMD susceptibility remain incompletely defined.  
Results  
To identify NMD substrates, we profiled four primary lung cell types with paired short- and long-read RNA-seq with and without inhibition of NMD with a SMG1 inhibitor. We detected 162,800 expressed transcripts with \>20,000 NMD susceptible isoforms per cell type. Overall, NMD degraded 14-18% of transcriptional output across these cell types, with strong enrichment in stress response and splicing-related pathways. Analysis of NMD susceptible transcripts identified splicing events that shifted transcription towards NMD, and we trained a deep learning sequence model that confirmed the importance of PTCs and uORFs as NMD triggers and that also identified NMD-promoting sequence features associated with translational readthrough.  
Conclusions  
We defined the landscape of NMD susceptible isoforms across primary human lung cell types and developed an accurate sequence-based model for predicting NMD susceptibility. Previously reported estimates that NMD degrades \~15% of all transcriptional output in human cells were confirmed across four lung cell types, and a sequence-based predictive model for NMD achieved high accuracy allowing for identification of sequence-based triggers of NMD. These data provide a transcriptome-wide resource of NMD targets in primary human lung cells that will accelerate studies of NMD biology and elucidate how disease-causing genetic variants alter transcript regulation in the lung.

Key Words: Nonsense-mediated decay (NMD), Long-read RNA-sequencing, RNA-seq, Alternative Splicing, Premature termination codon (PTC), Machine Learning

# **Background**

Nonsense-mediated decay (NMD) is a highly conserved mechanism in which RNA transcripts are targeted for degradation after ribosomal engagement. One of the functions of NMD is as a “proofreader” that identifies and degrades transcripts that contain premature termination codons (PTCs). However, NMD can be triggered for reasons beyond PTCs, including long 3’ UTRs[\[1\]](https://paperpile.com/c/lPcZkO/msH9D) and the presence of upstream open reading frames (ORFs)[\[2\]](https://paperpile.com/c/lPcZkO/argKs). In general, NMD-triggering events lead to stalled or delayed translation, and the RNA sequence characteristics that trigger NMD have not been fully described. Consequently, our ability to predict the extent to which specific transcripts will be degraded by NMD remains imperfect, despite the widespread use of heuristics such as the 50-nucleotide rule. The ability to predict NMD susceptibility of transcripts is important, because it has been shown that NMD is broadly active and degrades \~15% of the RNA output of protein coding genes[\[3\]](https://paperpile.com/c/lPcZkO/vdPEE).  
There is extensive evidence that the “proofreading” role of NMD has been adopted by some core cellular processes as a tool for regulating protein levels, particularly when rapid adjustments are needed. For example, NMD plays a major role in cellular stress[\[4\]](https://paperpile.com/c/lPcZkO/xuMXL), where it provides baseline suppression of stress response genes. When cells experience stress, NMD is inhibited, resulting in a rapid increase in stress response RNAs, providing clear evidence that cells have utilized NMD as a regulatory mechanism. Because NMD can be triggered by non-PTC-based sequence features, a subset of NMD-targeted transcripts, such as the master regulator of the integrated stress response \- *ATF4*, are capable of producing intact, functional protein[\[5\]](https://paperpile.com/c/lPcZkO/gD0AP).   
Because NMD acts at the transcript isoform level, accurately defining its substrates requires isoform-resolved transcriptomics. We hypothesized that integrating long-read RNA sequencing with NMD inhibition would systematically identify NMD-sensitive transcript isoforms across primary lung cell types and enable deep learning models to uncover the sequence principles governing isoform-level susceptibility to NMD. To study this hypothesis, we performed transcriptome-wide discovery of NMD susceptible transcripts in four different primary lung cell types – alveolar type 2 (AT2), large airway epithelial (LAE), fibroblast (FB), and microvascular endothelial (MV) – using short- and long-read RNA sequencing in normal culture conditions and in the presence of NMD inhibition. We identified tens of thousands of transcripts that are degraded by NMD, confirming that NMD is widespread. We observed significant enrichment of NMD susceptible genes involved in the integrated stress response and alternative splicing, as well as more cell type-specific pathways and processes. Using deep learning, we trained a highly accurate model to predict NMD susceptibility from transcript sequence, identifying novel RNA sequence features responsible for NMD, including stop codon-associated elements linked to translational readthrough.

# **Results**

## Section 1: Isoform Discovery via Long-read RNA-sequencing

We sequenced 26 samples to an average depth of 13 million aligned full-length non-chimeric (FLNC) reads, generating 341,638,920 total reads and identifying 162,800 expressed isoforms across 18,270 genes. Isoform length distributions were unimodal and centered near 2.5 kb, with minimal variation across cell types or treatments **(SF1)**. SQANTI analysis categorized 53.7% of transcripts as either full splice match (FSM \- 55,770 isoforms) or incomplete splice match (ISM \- 31,667 isoforms) to the GENCODE version 49 GTF; 44.4% of isoforms were novel (44,193 NIC and 28,045 NNC) with 1.9% falling into other transcript classes, including fusion and genic isoforms **(SF2)**. The median gene expressed five isoforms (mean 8.9, IQR 2-13, max 97), with 13,941 (76.3%) genes expressing two or more isoforms and 5,963 (32.6%) expressing ten or more.  
To assess the agreement between short-read and long-read RNA-sequencing data, we aggregated long-read isoform counts to the gene level and filtered to a common set of 28,651 genes across 26 matched samples. Sample-wise concordance was uniformly high across all 26 samples, with mean Pearson r \= 0.89 (range 0.83-0.91) and Spearman ρ \= 0.89 (range 0.85-0.90) **(Fig 1A)**. Per cell type Pearson means ranged from 0.88 (FB) to 0.90 (LAE) **(SF3)**. Long-read and short-read quantification are therefore highly concordant on a per-sample basis, regardless of donor, treatment, or cell type, validating the downstream use of both platforms.  
To examine how similar the isoform expression profiles were across cell types, we quantified cell type-specific expression in two ways: through differential expression analysis (difference in expression level between cell types) and identification of cell type-restricted expression (absence of expression in the other 3 cell types in dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) samples). Among 105,938 isoforms expressed at testable levels under DMSO, differential expression analysis by cell type identified 28,930 isoforms significantly associated with LAE, 22,131 associated with AT2, 21,429 associated with MV, and 18,422 associated with FB **(ST3)**. Spearman correlations using isoform log-CPM values showed that FB and MV were strongly correlated (ρ \= 0.80) while AT2 and LAE showed a more modest correlation with other cell types (ρ \= 0.51-0.64) **(SF4)**. Despite the large number of significant associations with cell type, cell type-restricted expression was uncommon (0.88-5.48% of each cell type’s expressed isoforms, **Fig 1B**). LAE contained the largest set of cell type-restricted isoforms (8,087), followed by AT2 (2,267), MV (2,015), and FB (1,131). Although only 27.8% (LAE) to 51.7% (MV) of cell type-restricted isoforms passed the expression filter required for differential testing, those that did all reached significance. Likewise, binary detection of expressed isoforms showed extensive sharing of transcript repertoires across cell types, with uniformly high Jaccard indices (0.78-0.85) **(SF4)**. Together, these findings indicate that lung cell types generally express the same set of isoforms but with variable levels of expression across cell types. 

## Section 2: NMD Response

To characterize the impact of NMD inhibition, we performed differential expression analysis at both the gene and isoform level. At the short-read gene level, analysis of 25,955 genes per cell type identified 3,122-6,753 significant genes, of which 49-67% had a log fold change (logFC) \>0 indicating that they were NMD susceptible **(Table 1\)**. At the long-read isoform level, analysis of 162,800 isoforms identified 24,803-35,336 significant isoforms per cell type, of which 90.9-92.0% were NMD susceptible **(Table 2\)**. Across all cell types, 34,387 unique NMD susceptible isoforms mapped to 7,105 unique genes; 19,803 (57.6%) were core targets shared across all cell types, while 9,154 (26.6%) were cell type-specific with a heavy concentration in LAE (83.4%) **(Fig 1C)**. Of the 3,736 unique short-read NMD susceptible genes, 62% (2,326) had an NMD susceptible isoform, while 4,779 additional NMD susceptible genes were detected only by long-read isoform analysis. The mean posterior logFC of NMD susceptible features was substantially larger at the long-read isoform level than at the short-read gene level (**Fig 1D**), demonstrating the benefit of isoform-resolved characterization of NMD substrates.   
For NMD susceptible isoforms, we evaluated their expression levels and the proportion of total gene expression arising from these isoforms, and we observed that they were concentrated at low isoform proportions – the majority fell below 50% of parent gene expression and a substantial fraction fell below 10% **(SF5)**. Despite their low relative abundance, these isoforms spanned more than four orders of magnitude of absolute expression. Between DMSO and SMG1i, these isoforms showed a clear upward shift in both proportion and absolute expression, confirming that the low-proportion baseline is due to ongoing NMD rather than constitutively low transcription. NMD susceptible isoforms remained detectable across a broad range of expression levels even in the DMSO condition indicating that NMD “tunes” the abundance of its targets rather than acting as a binary switch.  
To quantify the cell type-specificity of the NMD response, we identified isoforms and genes that were significant in only one cell type (per cell-type significance) and estimated the percentage of effect sharing between cell types (see Methods). At the isoform level, per-cell type specificity was higher in LAE (23.7%) compared to AT2, FB, and MV (0.8-3.4%), with the same pattern at gene resolution **(Fig 1E)**. Pairwise sharing was lowest for comparisons involving LAE (51-70% gene level; 35-72% isoform level), whereas the AT2/FB/MV trio showed substantially higher sharing (83-90% gene-level; 68-83% isoform-level) **(SF6)**. Together, these results indicate that while cell type-specific NMD targets can be identified, there is broad sharing of NMD effects across these four cell types. This finding contrasts with a recent report by Tan et al.[\[6\]](https://paperpile.com/c/lPcZkO/ePcqh) that concluded that NMD susceptible mRNAs are predominantly cell type-specific. We reanalyzed the Tan et al. RNA-seq dataset using the same mashr-based approach used throughout this study which revealed substantially greater cross-context sharing of NMD targets and general agreement between studies (supplemental results).  
Gene set enrichment analysis of the gene-level results showed a shared core of NMD-regulated pathways that were significant in three of the four cell types (**Table 3; ST1**): cellular response to topologically incorrect protein, cellular response to unfolded protein, and unfolded protein response. These pathways define a coherent ER-stress and integrated stress response program centered on the canonical PERK-ATF4-CHOP axis, with 75 leading-edge genes observed in all three pathways including *ATF3*, *ATF4*, *DDIT3*, *DNAJB9*, *EIF2AK3*, *ERN1*, *HERPUD1*, and *HSPA5* **(Fig 1F)**.  
To examine pathway enrichment at the isoform level, we repeated the enrichment analysis on the long-read results, scoring each gene by its largest-effect isoform **(Table 4; ST2)**. The most consistently and strongly enriched pathway was RNA splicing, and pathways related to cellular stress responses were also enriched (these included ER stress and the unfolded-protein response, amino-acid metabolism, activation and transport, and the oxidative-stress response). Another theme was protein and RNA homeostasis with enrichments in pathways related to the ubiquitin-proteasome system, ribosome biogenesis, cytoplasmic translation, and mRNA export. Beyond this shared core, each cell type harbored distinct pathway enrichments, indicating NMD regulates both shared and cell type-specific biological processes (supplemental results).   
The strong enrichment of RNA splicing pathways prompted us to investigate whether NMD preferentially targets RNA-binding proteins (RBPs). NMD susceptible genes were strongly enriched for RBPs listed in both the Gerstberger census (984 of 1542 were NMD targets; OR 3.3, p \< 10\-3), and the ENCODE roster of experimentally characterized RBPs (254 of 356 were NMD targets; OR 4.1, p \< 10⁻³; **SF7)**. Among the RBP functional classes listed, splicing regulators and core spliceosome components were most significantly enriched (splicing regulation OR 4.0; spliceosome OR 6.9), indicating that NMD preferentially regulates the splicing machinery itself **(ST3)**. Since the SR family of splicing factors is well known to use alternative splicing and poison exons to regulate their own protein levels, we examined this gene family and observed that 11 of 12 *SRSF* genes carried at least one NMD susceptible isoform. Across these 11 SR-protein genes, 6 genes triggered NMD via a poison cassette exon mechanism (*SRSF3*, *SRSF5*, *SRSF6*, *SRSF7*, *SRSF9*, *SRSF11*), 3 used intron retention (*SRSF1*, *SRSF2*, *SRSF10*), one triggered NMD via 3’ UTR splicing(*SRSF8)*, and one used gain of an internal exon (*SRSF4*) **(SF8-18)**. Together, these findings demonstrate that diverse alternative splicing mechanisms couple SR-protein expression to NMD, reinforcing the central role of NMD in the autoregulation of the splicing machinery.

## Section 3: Transcriptional Output Lost and Productive Isoform Response

To quantify the overall transcriptional output degraded by NMD, we quantified the percent transcriptional output lost at gene (PTL-gene) and isoform (PTL-iso) resolution. Across cell types.PTL-gene ranged from 11.1% (AT2) to 12.5% (MV) **(SF 20\)**, and PTL-iso ranged from 14.4% (AT2) to 18.2% (LAE) **(Fig 2A)**. Among NMD susceptible isoforms, PTL-iso was broadly distributed (median 60-67%, IQR 30-100%, **SF21**).  
One of the advantages of isoform-level characterization of NMD is that we can directly observe the productive and non-productive compartments of total gene expression. To study the effect of NMD inhibition on the productive compartment of gene expression (i.e. the “productive fraction”), we applied a custom normalization that corrected for the library inflation caused by the accumulation of NMD susceptible isoforms after SMG1 inhibition. This correction preserved gene rankings (Spearman ≥ 0.99 between the adjusted and uncorrected fold changes) and produced closely matched expression of non-NMD genes in DMSO and adjusted-SMG1i samples (Spearman ≥ 0.96; **SF23)**. To characterize the change in productive fraction, we performed differential expression analysis with mashr on genes containing at least one NMD susceptible isoform (see Supplemental Materials). Productive output was largely preserved: the median adjusted logFC was near zero in every cell type (AT2 \+0.14, LAE −0.04, FB \+0.10, MV \+0.05), with no significant change in roughly 80% of genes **(Fig 2B; ST4)**. We found 11 (FB) to 1337 (LAE) downregulated genes and 306 (FB) to 888 (LAE) upregulated genes **(ST4)**. Genes with increased productive output were enriched in the unfolded-protein response pathway (leading-edge genes including the ER chaperone *HSPA5* (BiP) and the UPR transducers *XBP1* and *EIF2AK3*) and for NF-κB/TNFα inflammatory signaling **(ST4)**, consistent with activation of the ER-stress/integrated stress and inflammatory response upon NMD inhibition. These findings suggest that while the 6 hour treatment predominantly captured mostly direct effects of SMG1 inhibition, there was evidence of downstream transcriptional responses in known NMD-regulated pathways.  
To distinguish the mechanisms underlying productive output changes following NMD inhibition, we applied a Kitagawa decomposition[\[7\]](https://paperpile.com/c/lPcZkO/le8ck) (see Methods). Across all NMD susceptible genes with a significant productive change, the level term was dominant in 87.4% of genes and the composition term in only 12.6%, indicating that change in productive output is governed primarily by transcriptional level rather than by the redistribution of isoforms **(ST4)**. This split was strongly direction-dependent. Genes that gained productive output were almost entirely level-driven (99.7% level, 0.3% composition), consistent with increased transcription raising productive and NMD susceptible isoforms together. The composition term instead concentrated in the genes that lost productive output. Among significant productive-down NMD genes, 31.9% were composition-dominated, showing that a shift of the isoform pool toward NMD susceptible transcripts is a meaningful driver of productive loss, yet a reduction in overall transcription (68.1%) remained the predominant driver. These findings were robust to our custom NMD-anchored normalization, with short-read gene-level induction added as an external transcriptional signal not derived from the long-read library **(ST4)**.  
Two distinct mechanisms partition all the productive-down genes. Composition-shift genes were specifically enriched for RNA splicing (OR 2.6, p \< 10⁻3) and SR/hnRNP factors (OR 6.8, p \< 10⁻³), together with snRNA-, rRNA- and mRNA-processing terms **(ST4)**. Notably, of the 12 canonical SR proteins, every significant change in productive output was a decrease (8 in LAE, 3 in AT2, 2 in MV). These factors regulate splicing transcriptome-wide, so their coordinated loss of productive output upon NMD inhibition could in turn propagate into broader splicing changes, consistent with prior reports[\[8\]](https://paperpile.com/c/lPcZkO/WqIrX). Transcriptional-repression genes were instead enriched for DNA replication (OR 2.5, p \< 10⁻3). and repair (OR 2.0, p \< 10⁻3). The direct, isoform-level NMD mechanism acts predominantly on the RNA-processing machinery, whereas the larger transcriptional-repression class reflects the secondary cell-cycle arrest following NMD inhibition.  
Three representative genes illustrate the distinct mechanisms underlying changes in productive output following NMD inhibition. The productive-up response is exemplified by the direct *ATF4* target *SHMT2*, which was NMD susceptible yet increased its productive output upon NMD inhibition (MV, 44.1 to 58.1 CPM; adjusted logFC \+0.39), in step with the overall gene induction (short-read logFC \+1.16; **Fig 2C)**. Because *ATF4* itself is an NMD target, NMD inhibition stabilizes *ATF4* transcripts, thereby activating its downstream transcriptional program and increasing productive *SHMT2* expression. The down-arm comprises two distinct mechanisms. The first is autoregulation of the splicing machinery which *SRSF2* illustrates directly. As its NMD susceptible isoform surged, its productive output fell (84 to 50 CPM; adjusted logFC −0.73) and its productive fraction collapsed from 91% to 26% **(Fig 2D)**. The second is transcriptional repression which *PCNA* shows. *PCNA* lost roughly half its productive output (LAE, 251 to 130 CPM; adjusted logFC −0.95), but its productive fraction moved only slightly (100% to 93%) and its short-read transcription fell in parallel (logFC −0.81), indicating the whole gene was transcribed less rather than its isoforms redistributed **(Fig 2E)**.

## Section 4: Attributing NMD Susceptibility to Specific Splicing Events via Isopair Analysis

In order to identify the splicing events that shift transcription towards NMD susceptible isoforms, we conducted analyses comparing the dominant expressed isoform to the most highly expressed NMD susceptible isoforms using the Isopair package ([https://github.com/peter4244/Isopair](https://github.com/peter4244/Isopair)), which identifies 12 different categories of splice events differentiating pairs of isoforms (**SF25**). This analysis was performed in 1,578 genes that had i)  3 expressed isoforms, ii)  1 NMD susceptible isoform, iii) 2 non-NMD isoforms, and iv) where the dominant non-NMD (reference) isoform accounts for \>= 25% of parent gene expression (**Fig 3A** and **SF26)**. This allowed for two pairwise comparisons between the Reference and two Comparator isoforms (NMD pair: NMD vs Reference and Control pair: non-NMD vs Reference) that identified splicing events that shift transcriptional output away from productive isoforms towards non-productive (NMD susceptible) isoforms. Since identification of PTCs requires a confident coding sequence region (CDS) call, some of the analyses below use a restrictive subset in which all three analyzed isoforms were present in the GENCODE reference (GENCODE reference set, n=132 genes). Other analyses used a less restrictive subset where only the dominant isoform needed to be in GENCODE, allowing for the CDS to be inferred in the novel isoforms through reference AUG tracing (reference AUG-traceable set, n=833, see **SF26** and Methods).  
We first examined the overall sequence similarity of the NMD and Control comparators to their reference isoform, noting that the NMD isoforms shared more sequence content with the reference, suggesting that NMD arises from targeted splicing events rather than disordered splicing (**Fig 3B**). We observed that skipped exon events were twice as frequent in NMD pairs compared to Controls (**Fig 3C**). Conversely, intron retention events were more common in Control pairs.

We examined structural features associated with NMD \- namely PTCs, 3’ UTR length, and uORFs. We first limited our analysis to the GENCODE reference set, and we observed a 24-fold enrichment of PTCs in NMD susceptible isoforms (36.4% vs 1.5% PTC rate, p \< 10⁻¹³) and a strong enrichment of stop codons upstream of the terminal EJC (**Fig 3D**). There was a strong dose-response relationship between upstream distance to the stop codon and the magnitude of the NMD response up to \~350nt (**SF31**).   
When we examined PTC-causing splice mechanisms in NMD isoforms, we observed that frameshift events were most common (54%), followed by in-frame PTCs (38%) and 3' UTR splicing (8%). Skipped exon was the most common event type (50% of PTC-causing events vs 14% in Controls, Fisher p \< 10⁻⁶) with A5SS also significantly enriched (13% vs 4%, p \< 0.05) (**Fig 3E and F**). We then stratified our analyses by the presence of PTCs, focusing our attention on the NMD susceptible isoforms for which a PTC was not identified (NMD+/PTC- isoforms). We observed that the NMD+/PTC- isoforms had longer 5’ UTRs and uORFs than both other groups (**Fig 4A and B**) with no significant difference in CDS length (**SF33**).   
We then analyzed the Reference AUG-traceable subset that includes novel isoforms. Since CDS calls in novel isoforms were derived from computational predictions from TD2[\[9\]](https://paperpile.com/c/lPcZkO/QLqjh), we evaluated for anti-PTC bias in TD2 CDS calls, which was clearly observed (**SF34-35**). We accordingly used reference AUG-tracing to define the CDS in the novel isoforms. With this approach, we identified PTCs in 92% of the NMD+ isoforms (768/833), and the 5’ UTR and longest uORFs were significantly longer in the NMD+/PTC- isoform subset (**Fig 4C and D**). For the 3’ UTR length analysis, there was some evidence for longer 3’ UTRs in the NMD+/PTC+ subset, but this was limited to the Reference AUG-traceable set only (**SF36**, see Supplemental Materials).

## Section 5: An Interpretable Predictive Model for NMD

Based on our Isopair analysis, the majority of NMD in our experiment was explainable by PTCs or features in the 5’ UTR. To investigate this further, we trained a deep learning model that predicted the likelihood of NMD from transcript sequence. The architecture of this model was designed to achieve both high predictive performance and interpretability, specifically for sequence near translational start and stop sites. The input data were structured as three distinct blocks of information related to 1000nt sequence windows around the translational start and stop sites and ORF structural data provided as a tabular matrix (**Fig 5A**). These data were fused in an internal layer which fed into an attention layer that allowed us to identify which ORF the model preferred for each isoform.   
The model had an AUC of 0.93 and AUPRC of 0.82 on the held-out test set (n \= 10,522 isoforms, 2,405 NMD susceptible; **Fig 5B**). Using Shapley values (SHAP), we observed that 55% of the predictive information came from the ORF structural data, with the remainder coming from sequence information, and the stop window sequence was roughly twice as important as the start sequence (**Fig 5C**). Of the individual ORF structural features, EJC count was by far the most important (**Fig 5D**).   
Sliding window mean SHAP values showed a pattern of increasing importance around the start and stop codons (**SF37**). Per-nucleotide SHAP suggests that the model learned Kozak sequence information (**Fig 5E**) at the start site, and at the stop codon the UGA codon increased the predicted value for NMD (**Fig 5F**). We confirmed this in direct analysis of isoform sequence, where UGA was more commonly used in NMD susceptible transcripts (58% vs 50%, OR 1.40, p \= 1.7×10⁻⁴², SF38). The UGA codon predisposes to translational readthrough, a trend that is also supported by the largest importance for U at the \+4 position (first base after the stop codon), a sequence feature that is also associated with readthrough[\[10\]](https://paperpile.com/c/lPcZkO/NHPlp).   
Interrogation of the attention layer in our model indicates which ORF the model uses to make the prediction for each isoform. While most of the model attention was focused on ORF0 (the most likely CDS), attention was more broadly distributed for NMD than Control isoforms (**SF39A and B**). In NMD+/PTC- isoforms, there was clear evidence that the model had learned the importance of 5’ UTR features as predictors of NMD in this subset, as the model devoted significantly more attention to isoforms with uORFs (**Fig 5G**; n \= 1,023 NMD+/PTC− against 6,344 NMD+/PTC+). Within the smaller reference AUG-traceable subset, the model also allocated roughly twice as large a share of its attribution to the start window as in NMD+/PTC+ isoforms (**SF40**; n \= 65 and 768\). However, overall predictive performance was substantially lower in NMD+/PTC− isoforms (AUC 0.64 against 0.94, though only 18 NMD+/PTC− isoforms fall in the held-out test set; **SF41**), indicating that this was a more challenging pattern to learn than PTCs.

For each transcript, five candidate ORFs are selected by priority (reference CDS \> TD2 CDS \> top-Kozak). CNN branches encode the sequence windows around each ORF's start and stop codons and a linear branch encodes five structural features; these fuse into a per-ORF embedding, and an attention layer aggregates the five ORFs into a transcript-level NMD prediction. (B) Performance on the held-out chr 1/3/5/7 paralog-free test set (n \= 10,522; 2,405 NMD susceptible): AUC 0.93, AUPRC 0.82 (PR curve inset). (C) KernelSHAP branch decomposition of the NMD-call signal over all 41,776 scored isoforms: Structural 54.6%, Stop 31.4%, AUG 14.0%. (D) Mean |SHAP| per structural feature over the same isoforms (5 DeepSHAP replicates); downstream EJC count dominates (0.940), \~3× the next feature. (E) Per-nucleotide signed SHAP around the start codon in NMD isoforms, where positive values push the prediction toward NMD; the model recovers a canonical Kozak preference (strong G preference at \-3 and \+4). (F) Signed SHAP around the stop codon. (G) Fraction of the model's attention on candidate uORFs in NMD+/PTC− (start lost), NMD+/PTC− (start retained), NMD+/PTC+, and Control isoforms; the model upweights uORFs in both NMD+/PTC− groups. \*p \< 0.05, \*\*p \< 10⁻³, \*\*\*p \< 10⁻⁴, \*\*\*\*p \< 10⁻¹⁰, n.s. otherwise (Mann-Whitney U). Abbreviations: TD2, TransDecoder2; CNN, convolutional neural network; AUC, area under the ROC curve; AUPRC, area under the precision–recall curve; SHAP, SHapley Additive exPlanation.

To benchmark our model's performance, we compared it to other predictive models for NMD \- NMDetective-B[\[11\]](https://paperpile.com/c/lPcZkO/funyy) and NMDEP[\[12\]](https://paperpile.com/c/lPcZkO/6PdWC), choosing for both the simpler rule-based models that could be replicated in our dataset. Our model had a lower Spearman correlation (0.73 versus 0.79 for both NMDetective-B and NMDEP), but its predictions had stronger correlation to the ground truth within NMD+/PTC+ and NMD+/PTC- classes (Supplemental Results and **SF43**).   
   

# **Discussion**

This study of NMD in primary lung cell types is the first long-read, transcriptome-wide description of NMD in full length isoforms, and it yielded multiple important findings. First, long-read RNA-seq is naturally suited to study NMD, and our isoform-level analysis identified stronger NMD effects than gene-level analysis. Second, NMD is widespread, and our study sheds light on mechanisms by which alternative splicing creates a large pool of NMD susceptible transcripts that provide an additional layer of regulatory control over protein levels. Third, in our four studied lung cell types, the effects of NMD were roughly evenly split between shared and cell type-specific effects. While NMD targets were enriched in multiple biological pathways, we observed strong and broad enrichment in alternative splicing and cell stress responses. Fourth, transcriptome-wide isoform level analysis combined with a novel pairwise isoform analysis allowed for plausible mechanistic attributions of the cause of NMD within each susceptible isoform which confirmed the dominant role of PTCs as NMD triggers, but it also identified roughly 10% of NMD susceptible isoforms in which 5’ UTR structure and uORFs appear to drive NMD. Finally, we developed sequence-based predictive models of NMD that are comparable to other highly accurate models while allowing for sequence-specific insight into mechanisms of NMD. Our analyses confirmed prior observations regarding the importance of PTCs, uORFs, and exon skipping in NMD and suggested novel links between NMD-associated sequence features and translational readthrough.   
This study generated short and long-read RNA-seq data from the same samples, allowing for direct comparison of the two technologies. At the gene level, the correlation between both technologies was \~0.9 across all studied cell types, indicating that current long-read technology has reached the stage where quantitative analysis of gene and isoform expression is practical. Furthermore, long-read analysis identified more effects (twice as many genes containing a significant isoform) and stronger effects than short-read, presumably due to the isoform-level analysis of a fundamentally isoform-specific phenomenon. Nonetheless, only \~60% of short-read identified genes are captured by long-read, and there are specific cases, such as very long genes that are not captured by the PacBio Kinnex technology, where short-read data provides additional information.   
Our study confirms previous reports that NMD is widespread. While Fair et al.[\[3\]](https://paperpile.com/c/lPcZkO/vdPEE) reported that 15% of the transcriptional output for protein coding genes is degraded by NMD, we confirmed a similar range of effects in our primary lung cell types (14-18% of transcriptional output degraded). NMD is most frequently discussed in two different scenarios \- the “rare mutation scenario” where PTCs arise from low frequency germline or somatic variants and the “AS-NMD” scenario where PTCs arise from the effects of alternative splicing. Our data provides additional evidence of the widespread presence of AS-NMD, and we implicate exon skipping and alternative 3’ splice site selection as two splice mechanisms that are significantly enriched in the NMD transcripts relative to dominant, protein productive isoforms.  
Among the pathways enriched in NMD targets, the most prominent across cell types were those related to the cellular stress response and RNA splicing. In our data, three overlapping ER-stress and unfolded protein response pathways reached significance in three of the four cell types, and leading edge analysis converged tightly on the canonical PERK-ATF4-CHOP axis. The cellular stress response has been previously linked to NMD, including the first transcriptome-wide profile of NMD substrates, which identified stress-response factors such as *ATF3* and *ATF4[\[2\]](https://paperpile.com/c/lPcZkO/argKs)*. The core integrated stress response factors *ATF4*, *ATF3*, and *CHOP* are direct NMD substrates whose mRNAs accumulate when the pathway is suppressed[\[4,13\]](https://paperpile.com/c/lPcZkO/RB6zA+xuMXL), and this pathway exemplifies how uORF-mediated NMD susceptible transcripts may produce functional protein under certain conditions. Quantitative proteomics has further shown this regulation is concentrated specifically on the PERK-ATF4 branch of the Unfolded Protein Response[\[14\]](https://paperpile.com/c/lPcZkO/HdkqC). Genes of this canonical axis ranked among the top NMD susceptible genes in all four primary cell types, indicating that NMD restrains the integrated stress response in primary human lung cells in the absence of stress signals.  
RNA splicing was also strongly enriched across all four cell types. The leading-edge genes were predominantly SR proteins, hnRNPs, and core spliceosomal components. Human SR-protein genes, along with many other splicing regulators, produce unproductive mRNA isoforms primarily via poison cassette exons, providing negative autoregulation of splicing-factor levels[\[15,16\]](https://paperpile.com/c/lPcZkO/FoG7X+Bb4aJ). The exons that trigger this decay are frequently ultraconserved and the same regulation extends to core spliceosomal proteins such as SmB/B′ (*SNRPB*), which we likewise identify in leading edge analysis from our data[\[17\]](https://paperpile.com/c/lPcZkO/geI3E). Our study provides a comprehensive characterization of NMD in SR-proteins, and we report that 11 of the 12 canonical SR proteins (*SRSF1-SRSF11*) express an NMD susceptible isoform in every cell type, and our pairwise analysis of isoform profiles demonstrated canonical poison exon mechanisms in six of the SR family genes and alternative PTC-inducing mechanisms for the other five. When we evaluated RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) broadly, we observed many instances of NMD with stronger enrichment in RBPs involved in regulation of splicing compared to those annotated as binding primarily in 3’ UTRs. This adds large-scale evidence supporting the recursive relationship between splicing and NMD, which seem to regulate each other[\[8\]](https://paperpile.com/c/lPcZkO/WqIrX).   
Our analysis provides a transcriptome-wide view of NMD that allows us to estimate the degree of sharing versus cell-type specific NMD activity. We observed a substantial amount of sharing of NMD effects across cell types (44.8% at gene-level, 57.6% at isoform-level). On its surface, this differs from the previous report by Tan et al.[\[6\]](https://paperpile.com/c/lPcZkO/ePcqh) which reported only 16-25% transcript-level overlap of UPF2-dependent NMD targets between human embryonic stem cells and neural progenitor cells, but it is more in line with the study by Palou-Marquez et al[\[18\]](https://paperpile.com/c/lPcZkO/G9P2p). However, re-analysis of the Tan et al. data using comparable methods yielded a 41-50% transcript-level overlap that is more similar to our results.   
NMD-susceptible isoforms that lacked a canonical PTC were distinguished by longer 5′ UTRs and longer upstream open reading frames (uORFs), consistent with the established role of uORFs, which occur in roughly half of human transcripts, as pervasive repressors of translation and steady-state mRNA abundance[\[19,20\]](https://paperpile.com/c/lPcZkO/cYm3+XaLC). Because ribosomes that terminate at a uORF stop codon undergo termination that the cell recognizes as premature, either upstream of a downstream exon-junction complex or at an abnormal distance from the poly(A) tail, uORF-containing mRNAs are well-documented endogenous NMD substrates independent of disease-associated PTCs[\[1,2,21\]](https://paperpile.com/c/lPcZkO/msH9D+argKs+Q2bE). The 5′ uORFs of ATF4 illustrate the regulatory potential of this mechanism, simultaneously rendering the transcript NMD-susceptible and licensing its stress-induced translational reinitiation, which suggests that the PTC-independent, uORF-associated NMD we observe may add a tunable layer of gene regulation in primary lung cells[\[5\]](https://paperpile.com/c/lPcZkO/gD0AP).  
Using a deep learning model, we could predict NMD susceptibility with high accuracy from isoform sequences and ORF-related annotations. Using interpretable AI measures, analysis of our model clearly supported the role of PTCs as the most important mechanism of NMD susceptibility, and it also confirmed the role of 5’ UTR length and uORFs as a secondary mechanism of NM. Shapley analysis of sequence features around stop codons suggests that NMD susceptible transcripts are also enriched for sequence elements that favor translational readthrough, such as increased use of the UGA stop codon as well as other supportive sequence features. This connection is interesting and yields many potential explanations, with one possibility that readthrough-favorable features may be triggering NMD by inducing ribosomal pausing \- but additional functional data would be required to investigate this further. Our model is competitive with the rule-based baselines presented in NMDetective[\[11\]](https://paperpile.com/c/lPcZkO/funyy) and NMDEP[\[12\]](https://paperpile.com/c/lPcZkO/6PdWC), but its sequence-based nature allows for more mechanistic interpretation and mechanistic hypothesis generation. Future work in this area will likely improve our understanding of how to use interpretable machine learning methods to differentiate causal mechanisms from purely associative correlations.  
	The major strength of this paper is the use of long read RNA-seq coupled with targeted inhibition of NMD using a small molecule inhibitor of SMG1. This paper reveals for the first time tens of thousands of specific NMD targets across four cell types, which are publicly available at (https://nmd-lungcells.castaldilab.org/). Our data indicate that our experiments achieved effective inhibition of NMD with relatively few off-target effects. However, there was some evidence of secondary responses to NMD inhibition that suggest that, at six hours, some downstream effects of NMD inhibition were evident in pathways heavily regulated by NMD. In the future, time series studies after NMD inhibition will allow for better delineation of direct and secondary effects. Analysis of four different primary lung cell types allowed for identification of a “core” set of NMD susceptible genes, and our findings of roughly equal proportions of shared and context-specific NMD fits into previous investigations of NMD across different cellular contexts. Our deep learning model confirms the ability to predict NMD susceptibility with good accuracy from post-spliced RNA sequence, and we demonstrate that Shapley analysis of these models can provide both high level and sequence-specific insight into potential functional mechanisms underlying NMD, though our novel observations require further functional confirmation. 

# **Conclusions**

This study provides the first transcriptome-wide, isoform-level description of nonsense-mediated decay across primary human cell types using long-read RNA-seq. Long-read RNA-seq is uniquely suited for studying NMD, an isoform-level phenomenon, and resolves stronger NMD effects than short-read data. We found NMD to be widespread with thousands of susceptible transcripts in protein-coding genes in every cell type. NMD impacts pathways related to alternative splicing and cell stress responses across all cell types and also affects many cell type-specific targets. Long-read sequencing also allowed for accurate sequence-based prediction of NMD susceptibility, which both confirmed the central roles of PTCs, uORFs, and exon skipping/inclusion, and generated new hypotheses linking NMD-associated sequence features to translational readthrough. These data establish a useful transcriptome-wide resource of NMD targets in lung cells, advance our understanding of the principles governing NMD susceptibility, and lay the foundation for investigating how genetic variation and disease alter RNA surveillance in the human lung.

# **Methods**

For the full length Methods, please see the Supplemental Materials. We studied four primary human lung cell types — alveolar type 2 (AT2), large airway epithelial (LAE), fibroblast (FB), and microvascular endothelial (MV) — isolated from human donors and cultured as previously described[\[22–25\]](https://paperpile.com/c/lPcZkO/z2hgA+QOhY5+QD0D+0VNm). To drive the accumulation of NMD substrates, we treated each culture with the SMG1 inhibitor SMG1i, or DMSO as a control, for six hours, and profiled every sample by both short-read (Illumina) and long-read (PacBio Kinnex) RNA sequencing. Long reads were aligned with minimap2[\[26\]](https://paperpile.com/c/lPcZkO/J6lE) and assembled and quantified with the PacBio Isocall pipeline (https://github.com/PacificBiosciences/isocall), and the resulting isoforms were classified against GENCODE 49 using SQANTI3[\[27\]](https://paperpile.com/c/lPcZkO/5dgp).  
To identify transcripts regulated by NMD, we tested for a SMG1i effect at the gene level (short-read) and the isoform level (long-read) with limma-voom, modeling cell type, treatment, and their interaction with a within-donor blocking term, and then jointly analyzed these cell type effects using multivariate adaptive shrinkage (mashr)[\[28\]](https://paperpile.com/c/lPcZkO/4fee). Genes or isoforms with a local false sign rate below 0.05 and a positive posterior log2 fold change — that is, increased upon NMD inhibition — were classified as NMD susceptible. We summarized the overall transcriptional burden of NMD as the percent of transcriptional output lost, and separately quantified how each gene's productive (non-NMD) isoforms responded once we removed the artifactual deflation caused by the accumulation of unproductive isoforms in the SMG1-inhibited state.  
To attribute NMD susceptibility to specific splicing events, we developed the Isopair package ([https://github.com/peter4244/Isopair](https://github.com/peter4244/Isopair)) for comparing pairs of full length isoform sequences with a “reference” and “comparator” isoform. Isopair enumerates twelve splice-event categories that distinguish each comparator from the reference and calls PTCs using the canonical 50-nt rule given an open reading frame (ORF). To recover occult PTCs that length-biased CDS predictors miss, we selected the ORF by reference AUG-tracing, a process by which we project the reference isoform's start codon onto the comparator's spliced sequence.  
Finally, we trained a deep learning, sequence-based model to predict NMD susceptibility directly from transcript sequence, representing each transcript as up to five candidate ORFs encoded by sequence windows flanking the start and stop codons together with ORF-level structural features, and evaluating it on held-out chromosomes (1, 3, 5, and 7). We interpreted the model with DeepSHAP and KernelSHAP[\[29\]](https://paperpile.com/c/lPcZkO/xJgu) and benchmarked it against the rule-based predictors NMDetective-B[\[11\]](https://paperpile.com/c/lPcZkO/funyy) and NMDEP[\[12\]](https://paperpile.com/c/lPcZkO/6PdWC). Full details are provided in the Supplemental Methods.
